title: Structured Outputs & Function Schemas
summary: Agents feed model output into code, and code can't reliably parse prose. Structured outputs — JSON mode, response schemas, and function/tool JSON Schemas — constrain the model to return machine-readable data. You validate that data (often with pydantic), handle hallucinated or wrong-typed fields, and retry on parse failure so a single bad generation never breaks the loop.

subtopics.title: Free text is unparseable for an agent
subtopics.explanation: A model that answers 'Sure! The order total is about $42, shipped Tuesday' gives a human everything but gives your code nothing reliable to key on — the phrasing, number format, and field order all vary run to run. Regexing prose is brittle and breaks the moment the wording shifts. This is the core reason agents demand a fixed, structured shape rather than natural language.
subtopics.example:
reply = "Sure! The order total is about $42.00, shipping Tuesday."
# fragile: breaks if wording, currency, or order changes
import re
match = re.search(r"\$([0-9.]+)", reply)
total = float(match.group(1)) if match else None
# works today, silently returns None tomorrow -> unreliable for a loop

subtopics.title: JSON mode and structured outputs
subtopics.explanation: Providers offer a JSON mode that forces syntactically valid JSON, and stronger 'structured outputs' that constrain generation to a supplied schema so the shape is guaranteed. You still parse and validate, but the odds of well-formed data jump dramatically. Requesting structured output is the first line of defense that makes the rest of an agent's parsing code sane.
subtopics.example:
import json

# pseudo-provider call requesting strict JSON
resp = client.chat(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract total and ship_day."}],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},  # force valid JSON
    temperature=0,                              # keep the shape stable
)
data = json.loads(resp.content)   # much safer than regexing prose
print(data["total"], data["ship_day"])

subtopics.title: Describe the shape with a function/tool JSON Schema
subtopics.explanation: A tool (function) is exposed to the model with a JSON Schema: its name, description, and a parameters object listing each field's type, whether it's required, and any enums. The schema is both documentation for the model and a contract your code can validate against. Getting the schema right is what makes the model emit exactly the arguments your function expects.

subtopics.title: Validate with pydantic
subtopics.explanation: Even with schemas, you validate the parsed data against a strict model so type errors, missing required fields, and out-of-range values are caught before they reach your logic. Pydantic turns loose JSON into a typed object and raises a clear error when the data doesn't conform. Validation is the boundary that keeps a bad generation from silently corrupting the rest of the agent's run.

subtopics.title: Handle invalid fields and retry on failure
subtopics.explanation: Models still hallucinate fields, swap types, or wrap JSON in prose, so production code parses defensively and retries with a corrective message when validation fails. A bounded retry loop that echoes the error back to the model recovers most failures without a human. This defensive parse-validate-retry pattern is what makes structured output dependable inside an agent loop.

foundations.overview: In an agent, the model's output is not the final product — it's data that flows into your code, another tool, or the next loop iteration. Natural language is fine for humans but disastrous for programs because its shape varies every run. Structured outputs solve this: JSON mode forces valid JSON, structured-output/schema modes constrain generation to a shape you specify, and function/tool JSON Schemas declare exactly what arguments a tool takes. You then parse the JSON and validate it — commonly with pydantic — so type mismatches, missing required fields, and hallucinated keys are caught at a clear boundary. Because models still err, you wrap this in a defensive parse-validate-retry loop that echoes validation errors back for self-correction. Together these techniques turn unreliable text into a dependable contract, which is the difference between a demo and a production agent.
foundations.formalDefinition: Structured output is model generation constrained to a machine-parseable format (typically JSON), optionally conforming to a supplied JSON Schema. A function/tool schema is a JSON Schema describing a tool's name, description, and parameters (types, required fields, enums). Validation is the step of checking parsed output against a strict type model; on failure the agent retries with corrective feedback up to a bound.
foundations.whyItMatters: Every downstream step in an agent — running a tool with the model's arguments, storing a result, deciding the next action — depends on data it can trust. Without structured output and validation, agents fail unpredictably and silently; with them, failures become explicit, catchable, and recoverable, which is the foundation of reliability.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the model as an intern filling out a form. Free text is the intern writing you a friendly paragraph; a JSON Schema is handing them a form with labeled, typed fields; validation is you checking the form for blanks and wrong entries before filing it; and the retry loop is handing it back with 'you left field X blank' until it's right.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Extracting structured records from documents, generating tool-call arguments the runtime executes, producing classification/verdict objects, populating database rows from unstructured input, and enforcing an API contract between an LLM step and the rest of a pipeline.
foundations.performanceImpact: Structured-output and low-temperature settings raise first-try validity, cutting the retry rate; since each retry is a full extra model call, higher validity directly reduces cost and tail latency, while validation adds negligible overhead compared with a generation.
commonUseCases: Generating tool-call arguments from a JSON Schema
Classification and verdict objects consumed by code
Enforcing a contract between an LLM step and a pipeline

commonMisconceptions.myth: JSON mode guarantees the data is correct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It guarantees syntactically valid JSON, not correct or complete data. Fields can be missing, wrong-typed, or hallucinated — you still validate against a schema/pydantic model.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A good prompt alone removes the need to validate.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Prompting lowers the failure rate but never to zero. Production code always parses defensively and retries, because one bad generation in a loop can corrupt everything after it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Structured outputs and function schemas are different features.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They're the same idea applied twice — a JSON Schema constrains the model's output, and a function/tool schema is just that schema describing a tool's arguments.

interactiveExamples.title: From fragile prose to validated JSON
interactiveExamples.explanation: Contrast pulling a number out of a sentence with regex against parsing structured JSON and validating it with pydantic. Only the second approach is safe to build a loop on.

code.code:
import json, re
from pydantic import BaseModel

# fragile: regex over prose
prose = "The total is about $42.00."
total_bad = float(re.search(r"\$([0-9.]+)", prose).group(1))

# robust: structured JSON + validation
class Result(BaseModel):
    total: float
    currency: str

structured = '{"total": 42.0, "currency": "USD"}'
result = Result(**json.loads(structured))

print("fragile:", total_bad)
print("validated:", result.total, result.currency)
code.caption: The regex works only for one exact phrasing; the validated model gives you a typed object you can rely on.

interactiveExamples.title: Parse-validate-retry with corrective feedback
interactiveExamples.explanation: A reusable helper that requests JSON, validates against a pydantic model, and on failure feeds the exact validation error back to the model so it can self-correct — bounded by a retry limit. A fake client simulates one bad then one good response.

code.caption: The first response fails validation ('yes' is not a bool); the corrective retry succeeds — recovery without a human.

codeLab.title: Build a validated extraction function
codeLab.instructions: Implement extract_order(raw_json: str) -> Order that parses a JSON string and validates it against a pydantic Order model with fields order_id: str, total: float, and priority: str constrained to one of 'low'/'medium'/'high'. It must (1) return an Order on valid input, (2) coerce a numeric string total like '42.00' to a float, and (3) raise ValueError (not a bare ValidationError) with a helpful message on invalid input. Complete the function so the harness passes.

    total: float
    priority: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]

def extract_order(raw_json: str) -> Order:

    # On any failure, raise ValueError with a clear message.
    ...

codeLab.testHarness:
ok = extract_order('{"order_id": "A-1", "total": "42.00", "priority": "high"}')
assert ok.total == 42.0 and ok.priority == "high"

# bad enum value -> ValueError
try:
    extract_order('{"order_id": "A-1", "total": 5, "priority": "urgent"}')
    raise AssertionError("should have raised")
except ValueError:
    pass

# malformed JSON -> ValueError

    extract_order('not json at all')
    raise AssertionError("should have raised")
except ValueError:
    pass
print("all tests passed")
hints: pydantic's model_validate_json both parses the string and validates the fields in one call.
Catch ValidationError for schema problems and a broad Exception for malformed JSON, re-raising both as ValueError.
Use `raise ValueError(...) from e` so the original cause is preserved in the traceback.

debuggingLab.title: The model wrapped JSON in prose and swapped a type
debuggingLab.scenario:
Your extraction agent worked in testing but crashes in production. The model started replying 'Sure! Here is the data:
```json
{"total": "42", "paid": "true"}
```' — prose plus code fences around the JSON, and both fields as strings instead of a number and a boolean. json.loads throws, and even after stripping the fences, downstream code that expects `paid is True` misbehaves because 'true' is a truthy string, not a bool.

buggyCode.code:
import json

def extract(reply: str) -> dict:
    data = json.loads(reply)          # crashes: reply has prose + ```json fences
    if data["paid"]:                  # 'true' (str) is always truthy!
        mark_paid(total=data["total"])  # data['total'] is a str '42', not 42
    return data

reply = 'Sure! Here is the data:\n```json\n{"total": "42", "paid": "false"}\n```'
extract(reply)  # boom, and even if parsed, 'false' would count as paid

debuggingLab.diagnosis: Two bugs compound. First, the response isn't pure JSON — it has conversational text and markdown fences, so json.loads fails on the whole string. Second, even after extracting the object, the fields are the wrong types: 'total' is a string and 'paid' is the string 'false', which is truthy, so `if data['paid']` is always True. Relying on raw json.loads plus dict access gives no type safety and no tolerance for surrounding prose.
debuggingLab.lesson: Never trust that model output is clean JSON of the right types. Extract the JSON object defensively (tolerating prose and fences), then validate with a typed model so 'false' becomes a real bool and '42' becomes a float. Better still, request structured-output/JSON mode and low temperature up front to make surrounding prose rare, and keep the extractor plus a bounded retry as the safety net.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Place structured output behind a single 'typed LLM call' boundary: a function that takes messages plus a pydantic model, requests structured/JSON mode, extracts the JSON block, validates, and retries with corrective feedback up to a bound before raising. Every agent step that needs data calls through this boundary, so parsing, validation, and retry logic live in one place instead of being reimplemented per tool. Downstream code receives typed objects only, never raw strings.
productionDeepDive.performance: Set temperature 0 and use provider structured outputs to maximize first-try validity, since each retry is a full extra model call that adds cost and tail latency. Keep schemas tight (fewer optional/free-form fields) so the model has less room to drift, and cache the immutable schema/system prefix with provider prompt caching to cut input token cost on repeated calls.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Bound retries (e.g. 2) and treat exhausted retries as a first-class failure the caller can route to a fallback model, a human, or a safe default — never an unhandled exception in the loop. Log the raw model output alongside the validation error so failures are reproducible. Make the retry message specific (echo the exact validation error) so the model self-corrects instead of repeating the same mistake.
productionDeepDive.observability: Emit metrics for first-try validity rate, retries per call, and final failure rate, broken down by schema and model version, so a silent regression (e.g. a model update that starts adding prose) is visible immediately. Capture a sample of raw outputs that failed validation for offline analysis, and alert when the retry rate crosses a threshold since it directly drives cost.
productionDeepDive.security: Validation is a security boundary: reject unexpected/extra fields (forbid extras in the pydantic model) so a hallucinated or injected key can't reach your logic, constrain strings that become tool arguments (e.g. enums, length limits, allow-lists), and never eval or directly execute model-provided values. Treat model output as untrusted input exactly like a user request.
productionDeepDive.cost: The dominant cost lever is the retry rate: raising first-try validity from, say, 85% to 99% removes a large fraction of second calls. Structured-output mode, low temperature, tight schemas, few-shot examples, and prompt caching of the fixed prefix together minimize both the number of calls and the tokens per call.

caseStudies.problem: An agent extracting invoice fields from PDFs intermittently crashed the pipeline: the model sometimes wrapped JSON in explanatory prose and occasionally returned amounts as strings, causing json.loads failures and downstream arithmetic bugs on 'total'.
caseStudies.solution: They introduced a typed LLM-call boundary using provider JSON mode at temperature 0, a defensive JSON-block extractor to tolerate stray prose, pydantic models with strict types and forbidden extra fields, and a two-retry loop that echoed validation errors back to the model.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: The retry loop adds up to two extra model calls on the rare failure and a little latency, and maintaining pydantic schemas is ongoing work; in exchange the pipeline stopped crashing and bad extractions became explicit, logged events instead of silent corruption.
caseStudies.lessons: Guarantee JSON syntax with the provider, but never assume field types or the absence of prose — validate everything, and make exhausted retries a routed failure, not an exception.

checkpoints.prompt: What does provider 'JSON mode' actually guarantee?
options: The data is correct and complete
The output is syntactically valid JSON
Every field matches your pydantic model
checkpoints.explanation: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON syntax only. Fields can still be missing, wrong-typed, or hallucinated, so you must validate the parsed data against a schema/pydantic model.

checkpoints.prompt: This 'validated' extraction still lets bad data through. What's wrong?
checkpoints.code:
import json
data = json.loads(model_reply)
if data["paid"]:            # model returned {"paid": "false", ...}
    ship_order(data["order_id"])
options: 'paid' is the string 'false', which is truthy, so the check always passes; no type validation was done
You cannot index a parsed dict
checkpoints.explanation: json.loads gives no type safety. The string 'false' is truthy, so the guard always passes. Validate with a typed model (paid: bool) so 'false' coerces to False or the data is rejected.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this pydantic validation print?
checkpoints.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel
class M(BaseModel):
    n: int
print(M(n="7").n + 1)
checkpoints.explanation: Pydantic coerces the numeric string '7' to the int 7, so 7 + 1 = 8. Coercion is why validation both cleans and type-checks loosely-typed model output.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the retry so the model gets the specific error and can self-correct.
checkpoints.explanation: Echoing the exact exception `{e}` back tells the model precisely what to fix (e.g. which field was the wrong type), which makes the corrective retry far more likely to succeed than a generic 'try again'.

theory.question: Why do agents need structured outputs instead of natural-language responses?
theory.directAnswer: Because an agent's output is consumed by code, tools, or the next loop step, not just a human. Natural language varies run to run and can't be parsed reliably, whereas structured output (JSON conforming to a schema) gives a fixed, machine-readable contract the rest of the system can depend on.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Structured output is model generation constrained to a parseable format like JSON, optionally conforming to a supplied schema, so downstream code can extract fields deterministically.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Programs need stable field names and types; regexing prose is brittle and breaks when wording shifts, causing silent failures inside a loop.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You request JSON mode or structured outputs, optionally supply a JSON Schema (also used for tool arguments), parse the result, and validate it against a typed model such as pydantic before using it.

theory.whyImportant: It's the boundary between a demo that works on one phrasing and a production agent whose every step can trust the data it receives.
theory.realWorldExample: An invoice agent returns {"total": 42.0, "currency": "USD"} instead of a sentence, so the pipeline can total, store, and route it without fragile text parsing.

followUps.question: Does structured output remove the need to validate?
followUps.answer: No. It guarantees the format (and often the shape) but not correct or complete data; you still validate types, required fields, and ranges.

followUps.question: How does this relate to function/tool schemas?
followUps.answer: A tool's parameter JSON Schema is the same mechanism — it constrains the arguments the model emits so your function receives exactly what it expects.

theory.question: How do you handle a model that returns invalid or wrong-typed structured output?
theory.directAnswer: Parse defensively, validate against a strict typed model, and on failure retry a bounded number of times with a corrective message that echoes the exact validation error; if retries are exhausted, route to a fallback or human rather than crashing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A parse-validate-retry pattern that treats each model generation as untrusted and recoverable rather than assumed correct.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Even with JSON mode and good prompts, models occasionally add prose, swap types, omit required fields, or hallucinate keys — one such failure can corrupt everything after it in a loop.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Extract the JSON object (tolerating stray prose/fences), validate with pydantic, and on ValidationError append the assistant's bad output plus a user message quoting the error and asking for valid JSON only, looping up to a max_retries cap before raising a handled failure.

theory.whyImportant: It converts unpredictable, silent failures into explicit, mostly self-healing events, which is essential for an agent that runs unattended.
theory.realWorldExample: A triage agent returned needs_human as the string 'yes'; the retry echoed the type error, and the second attempt returned a real boolean — recovered with no human involvement.

followUps.question: Why bound the retries?
followUps.answer: Each retry is a full extra model call adding cost and latency, and some inputs will never validate; a cap plus a fallback prevents runaway loops.

followUps.question: Why echo the exact error back?
followUps.answer: A specific error (which field, which type) lets the model fix the precise problem, far more effective than a generic 'that was wrong, try again'.

scenario.question: An extraction agent has a 12% parse-failure rate in production, spiking cost from retries. How would you diagnose and drive it down?
scenario.directAnswer: Instrument first-try validity, retries per call, and failure reasons by schema/model; then attack the top causes — enable structured-output/JSON mode, set temperature 0, tighten and simplify the schema, add few-shot examples, and make the retry message quote the exact error. Keep a bounded retry plus fallback as the safety net.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reliability-and-cost tuning problem where malformed outputs trigger extra model calls.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: High temperature, loose prompts, over-complex schemas, or a model update that started adding prose all lower first-try validity, and every failure costs a retry.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Log raw failing outputs and validation errors, group them to find the dominant failure mode (prose wrapping vs type errors vs missing fields), and apply the matching fix — mode/temperature for prose, tighter types/enums for type errors, required-field emphasis and examples for omissions.

scenario.whyImportant: It ties structured output directly to production cost and shows the metrics-driven, root-cause approach rather than blindly increasing retries.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs showed most failures were prose-wrapped JSON after a model update; enabling JSON mode at temperature 0 plus a defensive extractor dropped failures from 12% to under 1% and cut the retry bill sharply.

followUps.question: Why not just raise max_retries to hide the failures?
followUps.answer: That multiplies cost and latency and masks a root cause; fixing first-try validity is cheaper and more robust than paying for more retries.

followUps.question: How would you catch a future regression fast?
followUps.answer: Alert on the first-try validity metric per model version so a provider update that reintroduces prose is caught before it inflates cost.

coding.question: Write a defensive parser that extracts the first JSON object from a possibly-prose-wrapped string and validates it against a pydantic model, raising ValueError on any failure.
coding.thoughtProcess: Model output may include prose or code fences, so I first extract the first {...} block with a DOTALL regex, then let pydantic parse-and-validate that block. I catch both the 'no object found' case and validation/JSON errors, re-raising them as a single ValueError so callers have one exception type to handle.
lineByLine: The DOTALL regex grabs the first {...} span so surrounding prose and code fences are ignored.
If no object is found at all, we fail fast with a clear ValueError.
model_validate_json parses the extracted block and validates types in one step, coercing where sensible.
ValidationError (schema issues) and JSONDecodeError (malformed JSON) are both re-raised as ValueError so callers handle one type.
`from e` preserves the underlying cause for debugging.
The __main__ block shows a prose+fence-wrapped input being cleanly parsed to a typed Verdict.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the text for the regex scan and parse.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the matched substring and parsed object.

followUps.question: How would you wrap this in a retry loop?
followUps.answer: Call the model, run parse_validated, and on ValueError append the assistant output plus a corrective user message quoting the error, retrying up to a bound before raising.

followUps.question: What's a limitation of the regex approach?
followUps.answer: A greedy {.*} can over-match if the text contains multiple objects or nested braces; for robust cases prefer provider structured outputs so the whole response is the object.

keyTakeaways: Agents consume output with code, so free text is unreliable — use structured (JSON) outputs with a fixed shape.
JSON mode guarantees valid syntax; structured outputs and JSON Schemas constrain the shape and tool arguments.
Always validate parsed output (e.g. pydantic) to catch wrong types, missing required fields, and hallucinated keys.
Wrap generation in parse-validate-retry: echo the exact validation error back so the model self-corrects, bounded by a max-retry cap.
In production, put this behind one typed-call boundary, track first-try validity, and treat exhausted retries as a routed failure — not a crash.
